```{r setup}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
storemax <- read_csv("storemax.csv") |>
  mutate(region = factor(region,
    levels = c("Southeast","Northeast","Midwest","West")))
```

# Why Regression? {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

## The workhorse of business research

- Open any issue of *JMR*, *Marketing Science*, or *JM*: the headline
  evidence is very often a **regression table**
- Research questions of the form:
  *"How is Y related to X, holding everything else constant?"*
- Today: **run it and read it**. Tomorrow: interrogate it.

::: notes
Show 2–3 journal abstracts/tables here (screenshots).
Pick your own go-to papers; read one DV + one coefficient aloud.
:::

## When to use multiple regression

- **Outcome (Y):** one continuous variable
- **Predictors (X):** any mix — continuous, categorical, many of them
- **Question:** association between each X and Y, *adjusting for the others*
- Not (yet) a causal claim — that conversation is tomorrow

## Meet StoreMax (our running example)

A national retail chain, 400 stores, one week of data:

```{r}
glimpse(storemax)
```

::: notes
This dataset follows us all weekend. Every method we learn
interrogates this same company.
:::

# A Little Theory (No Proofs) {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

## The model

$$\text{sales}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{ad\_spend}_i + \beta_2\,\text{price}_i + \varepsilon_i$$

- The model describes the **conditional mean** of Y given the Xs
- $\beta_k$: expected change in Y for a one-unit change in $X_k$,
  **holding the other Xs constant**
- "Holding constant" is the entire point of *multiple* regression

## How the line is chosen: OLS

- OLS picks the $\beta$s that minimize the sum of **squared residuals**
- Residual = actual − predicted: what the model missed

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(storemax, aes(ad_spend, sales)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Ad spend ($000/week)", y = "Weekly sales (units)")
```

::: notes
One intuitive picture; no derivation. "Best" has a precise meaning —
we give it a name (BLUE) tomorrow.
:::

# Running It in R {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

## `lm()`: one line

```{r}
m1 <- lm(sales ~ ad_spend + price + store_size, data = storemax)
```

That's it. The work is in **reading** what comes back.

## Anatomy of `summary()` — the whole output

```{r}
summary(m1)
```

::: notes
Spend real time here. Walk every line on the next slides.
:::

## Anatomy, line by line

| Piece | What it is | What it is **not** |
|---|---|---|
| `Estimate` | the fitted $\beta$ | a causal effect |
| `Std. Error` | uncertainty in $\beta$ | the spread of Y |
| `t value`, `Pr(>|t|)` | test of $\beta = 0$ | effect size |
| `R-squared` | share of **variance** explained | share of sales explained |
| `F-statistic` | all slopes = 0, jointly | model "correctness" |

## Output → Sentence {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
tidy(m1) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 2)))
```

**What we can now say:**

> "Holding price and store size constant, each additional $1,000 of weekly
> ad spend is associated with roughly ___ additional units sold
> (b = ___, p ___ )."

**Fill in the blanks. Every number in the table has a sentence.**

## Mis-interpretation check ❌

Would a reviewer let these through?

1. "Ad spend **drives** sales up by 100 units." 
2. "The model **explains 60% of sales**."
3. "Price is not significant, so price **has no effect**."

::: notes
(1) causal verb from observational data; (2) variance ≠ level;
(3) absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. Recurring segment —
same game appears on quizzes.
:::

# Categorical Predictors {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

## Dummy variables: region

```{r}
m2 <- lm(sales ~ ad_spend + price + store_size + region,
         data = storemax)
tidy(m2) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 1)))
```

- R picks a **reference category** (first level: Southeast)
- Each coefficient = that region **vs. the reference**, holding the rest constant

## Output → Sentence

> "Compared with Southeast stores (the reference), Northeast stores sell
> about ___ more units per week, holding ad spend, price, and store
> size constant."

- Changing the reference changes the coefficients, **not the model**
- `relevel()` demo: same fit, different comparisons

## Standardized vs. unstandardized

```{r}
m2_std <- lm(scale(sales) ~ scale(ad_spend) + scale(price) +
             scale(store_size) + region, data = storemax)
```

- Unstandardized: real units → best for **substantive** sentences
- Standardized: SD units → comparing **relative importance** within a model
- Never compare standardized βs **across** different samples/models
